summary.text: Today 也 means “also” or “as well” and has classical grammatical uses. Its ancient pictorial origin is disputed; claims that the graph was confused with 它 are separate from, and do not resolve, those origin proposals.

formation.text: The whole graph is treated as pictographic, but its referent is disputed and no internal component split is supported. The Shuowen account interprets it as female genitalia; another account interprets it as a snake. The Shuowen commentary and the snake account each propose that the graph was later borrowed for grammatical words: a sign for an object could be reused if the object’s name sounded like those words. Neither depicted object nor the proposed name-to-word sound match is established. A child crying, a vessel or funnel, and a mouth-related form are other reported proposals, not verified explanations.

history.text: The selected bronze-style and seal-style forms are modern redrawings, not images of dated artifacts. The bronze-style drawing has an uncertain period label; neither drawing establishes what the ancient graph depicted.

A secondary report says 也 was distinct from 它 in early scripts and that the two became confused only after Emperor Wu of Han. This reported graphic confusion does not settle the graph’s origin, and its underlying paleographic argument has not been verified here.

uncertainties.text: The original referent and earliest securely documented occurrence of the graph remain unresolved. The proposed connection with 啼 is reported through a secondary summary; the underlying paleographic argument was not inspected.
The proposed borrowing accounts cannot be checked against the pictured object’s name or pronunciation, which are not established.
The evidence does not establish a chronological order or semantic path among particle, copular-like, affirmative, focus, and “also” uses.

senses.text: 也 has classical grammatical uses. The earliest securely dated occurrence is unsettled; general glosses and transmitted examples do not establish it.
Modern Chinese uses 也 as an adverb meaning “also” or “as well.” Dictionary glosses attest the use but do not establish when or how it developed from particle uses.

senses.period: pre-Qin texts; precise dating unresolved here
senses.text: A grammatical analysis identifies copular use in the Guodian corpus and proposes a path from focus particle to copula. This concerns the word’s grammatical use, not the graph’s origin, and does not establish a dated sequence here.

limitations.text: The evidence does not establish chronology among particle, copular-like, affirmative, focus, and “also” uses, so no semantic-development links are asserted.
The Shuowen commentary and a character database propose borrowing the graph for function words. The pictured object, its name, and the proposed sound match are not established.
Comparisons with Tibetan and 唯 are reported as hypotheses; their primary arguments and sound correspondences are not established here.

items.period: Spring and Autumn label on a modern drawing; Commons flags the time period as needing clarification
items.tradition: Bronze-script style; modern SVG redraw attributed to Xiaoxuetang source material
items.caption: A modern redraw labeled as a bronze-style form of 也. Its outline does not establish the graph’s original referent, and the period label is uncertain.
items.alt: A black, open forked form at the top joins a shallow crosswise stroke and a long curving line that descends and bends to the right.
items.selection_reason: Shows a candidate early-script form relevant to 也’s disputed origin. Its redraw history includes an earlier misidentification as 它, so the resemblance does not settle the graph’s identity or meaning.
items.rights: Public domain release of the modern SVG representation, as stated on the Commons description page.

items.period: Shuowen seal-script style, associated with the Eastern Han lexicographic tradition; modern vector redraw
items.tradition: Small-seal/Shuowen-style script; modern Inkscape vector drawing
items.caption: A modern redraw of 也 in the seal-script style associated with the Shuowen tradition. It illustrates the transmitted form, not proof of the referent proposed in that account.
items.alt: A black seal-style form with a branched upper shape, a broad central enclosure, and a long curving lower stroke.
items.selection_reason: Provides a visual reference for the form connected with the Shuowen account, whose proposed referent remains an interpretation rather than an established origin.
items.rights: Public domain release stated on the Commons file page.

limitations.text: Both images are modern vector redrawings, not images of dated artifacts. The bronze-style drawing’s period label is uncertain, and neither form resolves the competing proposals for what 也 originally depicted.
